lesson.title: Why Other People Change Us: Social Influence Theory
lesson.summary: Social influence theory is the broad framework psychologists use to explain how the presence, opinions, and actions of other people, whether real or merely imagined, shape an individual's thoughts, feelings, and behavior.
lesson.body:
Social norms, discussed in the previous section, describe what the shared rules of a group actually are. Social influence theory asks the next, related question: through what psychological mechanisms do those norms, and other people more generally, actually change us? The answer turns out to matter quite a bit, because not all influence works the same way, and understanding the differences helps explain why some changes in behavior are shallow and temporary while others become genuine, lasting shifts in belief.

A useful and widely referenced framework comes from Herbert Kelman, who in 1958 distinguished three separate processes of social influence. Compliance is the most surface level: a person goes along with a request or expectation to gain a reward or avoid a punishment, such as social disapproval, without any real private change in belief, meaning the behavior is likely to stop as soon as the surveillance or incentive disappears. Identification occurs when a person adopts a belief or behavior because they value their relationship with the person or group asking for it, for example dressing or speaking a certain way to fit in with an admired social group, a change that lasts only as long as that relationship or group membership feels important. Internalization is the deepest level, occurring when a person genuinely accepts a belief or value as their own, integrating it into their existing value system so that it persists even without any social pressure, reward, or relationship maintaining it.

Another influential model, Bibb Latane's social impact theory from the early 1980s, describes influence almost like a physical force acting on a person, one that grows stronger with the strength, meaning the importance or status, of the source, the immediacy, meaning closeness in time and space, of the source, and the number of sources exerting the influence. Latane also proposed that the effect of adding more sources shows diminishing returns, meaning the difference between one persuasive voice and two is larger than the difference between, say, nine voices and ten, a pattern often compared to the way each additional light bulb adds less noticeable brightness to an already well lit room.

Together, these frameworks explain that social influence is not one single thing but a family of related processes operating at different depths, from shallow public compliance to genuine internalized change, and shaped by how strong, close, and numerous the sources of influence are. This general theory of influence underlies the more specific phenomena covered next in this unit, starting with persuasion, the deliberate use of communication to change other people's attitudes.
